passages.title: Passage 1
passages.instructions:
Questions 1–40

You should spend about 60 minutes on Questions 1–40, which are based on the reading passage below.
passages.body:
Sustainable Fisheries Governance

A Sustainable fisheries governance seeks to align harvest levels with stock productivity so marine ecosystems continue supplying food and livelihoods. International frameworks set target reference points based on maximum sustainable yield, yet data-poor fisheries lack reliable biomass estimates. Regional bodies allocate quotas among member states, often amid contested historical rights and shifting distributions of species under climate change. The author argues that governance must integrate ecological science with transparent decision rules that stakeholders can audit when allocations become politically charged. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

B Rights-based management assigns secure shares of allowable catch to fishers, cooperatives, or communities, creating incentives to steward stocks rather than race to land fish before rivals. Individual transferable quotas dominate some industrial fleets, while territorial user rights suit small-scale nearshore operations. Critics warn that consolidating shares in corporate hands can marginalise artisanal fishers unless caps and community set-asides protect access. Monitoring costs remain substantial, particularly where vessels transship at sea beyond coastal patrol range. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

C Ecosystem-based approaches limit bycatch of seabirds, turtles, and non-target fish through gear modifications such as circle hooks and illuminated nets. Closed areas protect spawning aggregations and nursery habitats, trading short-term catch reductions for long-term recruitment gains. Models coupling predator-prey dynamics suggest single-species targets may still overfish forage fish that seabirds depend on. Managers increasingly adopt harvest control rules that automatically reduce quotas when biomass indicators fall below precautionary thresholds tied to peer-reviewed assessments. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

D Illegal, unreported, and unregulated fishing drains billions of dollars annually and undermines legal fishers who comply with rules. Port state measures deny landing rights to suspect vessels, while satellite automatic identification system analytics flag gaps consistent with transshipment or disabled transponders. DNA barcoding of fillets helps trace mislabelled products through retail supply chains. Nevertheless, enforcement gaps persist in flags of convenience registries and on the high seas where jurisdiction fragments across overlapping mandates and limited naval capacity. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.

E Subsidies that lower fuel costs or finance vessel construction can perversely encourage overcapacity, negating conservation reforms unless governments redirect funds toward monitoring and stock recovery. World Trade Organization negotiations have sought disciplines on harmful subsidies, though implementation timelines stretch across electoral cycles. Development agencies promote value-added processing and cold chains so coastal economies benefit without expanding effort. The writer contends that trade policy and fisheries policy must be coordinated rather than siloed in separate ministries with conflicting mandates. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes.

F Climate-driven range shifts force renegotiation of access agreements when cod or mackerel move across erstwhile boundaries. Indigenous peoples assert customary harvesting rights that predate modern quota systems, challenging simplistic privatisation narratives. Gender dimensions matter because women dominate processing sectors affected by export bans during stock collapses. Participatory co-management experiments in tropical reef fisheries pair local ecological knowledge with seasonal closures enforced by community patrols, sometimes outperforming top-down bans that lacked legitimacy on the water. Longitudinal studies remain essential before drawing firm conclusions about causal mechanisms and durable outcomes. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality.

G Looking ahead, sustainable governance will depend on adaptive institutions that update rules as oceans warm and acidify. Open data platforms sharing catch and effort in near real time could deter cheating and improve models. If consumers demand verified sustainability labels without funding traceability, the author believes green marketing will outpace genuine reform. Holistic programmes combining rights reform, ecosystem protections, subsidy realignment, and equitable access offer a more credible blueprint than single-instrument fixes repeated each diplomatic season. Scholars caution that cross-national comparisons require careful attention to institutional context and data quality. Policy evaluations therefore depend on transparent reporting and independent replication of key results.
